messages.author: bca8b8861698c94c
messages.subject: web design
parts:
I am trying to use the Program DISTANCE to estimate population
densities of nocturnal rodents (mice and voles) in four vegetation
communities in the Southern Rocky Mountains. I am inheriting a web
design following Parmenter et al., 2003 and using the Program DISTANCE
to estimate density. We have caught mice and voles 4 consecutive
nights during a trapping session (mark/recapture). We have 3 trapping
sessions to look for temporal changes. I am looking for a couple of
insights into the Properties by which to enter the data. I enter the
data in a point-center model and as clusters of first captures for a
trapping session. I am pretty sure this is appropriate. However, I am
not sure how to enter "no captures" in a particular ring for a
particular trapping session. In the program it can be entered as 0
(in which it calculates a density that averages 0 into cluster sizes)
or -1 (in which a "no capture " ring is not used to average cluster
size in the analysis. Using one approach or the other gives very
different numbers.

Has anyone used this trapping design and program and has advice on the
best way to proceed? Thanks for your help.

Thanks,
Barry Rosenbaum

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: web design
parts:
Barry (and Distance sampling list):

There have been a number of queries to this list about formatting
trapping web data for analysis in Program Distance. The most recent
answer was provide by Dr. Thomas on 15 September of this year.
(http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/cgi-bin/webadmin?A2=ind0509&L=DISTANCE-SAMPLING&P=R307&I=-3&X=4DBD493CEAC91402D7&Y=eri...%40mcs.st-and.ac.uk).

Entry of trapping web data is very similar to entry of point transect
data, as that is the method by which data are analysed to produce
density estimates. There are 2 forms of inquiry that will be of
interest in getting entered into Distance:

1) First, you should consult the sample projects that came with your
download of Distance. Both the "house wren" and "songbird" sample
projects show data gathered from point transects, so their format are
applicable to the entry of trapping web data. Note particularly the
recognition of no detections at a point transect (web) during a sampling
event. This occurred on Point 5 of Region (stratum) 0 in the "house
wren" project, as well as Point 17 of Pasture 1 in 1980 in the
"songbird" project. Note that there is no distance recorded associated
with the lack of detection (or capture). Providing a distance of 0
implies an animal was detected at the sampling point (or centre of the
trapping web). As you note, this has considerable significance for your
detection function. You really, really, do not want to enter a distance
zero if nothing was detected.

2) You will want to acquaint yourself with entering distances in
intervals (also know as binned data). Data from the sample projects I
describe above are all continuous data (ungrouped). However, as your
traps are laid in concentric rings, distances are not continuous, but
rather constrained to the number of rings of traps you laid out.
Consult p.94 (Chapter 8) of the Distance users guide for version 5 beta
4 for a discussion of entering binned data.

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: web design
parts:
Barry:

I don't believe the concept of clusters applies with rodents captured in
a trapping web. The animals were captured as individuals, not detected
as a herd of mice roaming across your study site. There is no purpose
served by estimating cluster sizes of animals in this type of study.
The sampling protocol dictates much of how data are analysed. Given the
data were collected as individuals, the data should be analysed in that
manner. I can't fathom an advantage to treating the data as clusters;
do you have a reference for this method you describe?

Unless there is a compelling reason to treat the data in a manner
dissimilar to the manner in which they were collected, you should treat
the detections as individual observations.

> >Conceptually, do you think it would be better to run each animal I
> >catch at a trap as an individual observation (so multiple data entries
> >of 1 at each trap distance with a total potential of 12) or treat each
> >number of animals trapped at a distance as a cluster. If I treat the
> >data as a cluster (which I believe at least some others have done),
> >would no animals trapped at a particular distance be considered a
> >missing cluster size (in which case I would use -1 as the observation
> >entry and use size bias method in modelling expected cluster size) or
> >as a zero cluster size (in which case I would use 0 as the observation

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: web design
parts:
Barry: I'm reasonably convinced you are headed in the wrong direction
with the cluster idea. I was one of the analysts involved in the
Parmenter et al> (2003) work, and I didn't invoke cluster size for
Sherman traps that could only catch a single individual during a set.
Perhaps you are confusing cluster size with multiple animals being
captured in a single ring by a number of traps on that ring (i.e.,
binning of data). For rodent data such as yours, you needn't be
concerned with cluster size, and you should analyse your data as
individual encounters.


Barry Rosenbaum wrote:

> >I agree with you conceptually. I have looked through the publications
> >I used in designing the study and cannot find the reference to
> >clusters used in the analysis that I am almost sure was there. It
> >would have been in a paper by Parmenter. I will keep looking.
> >However, if you look at Anderson et al., 1983 (Ecology 64:674 - 680).
> >it would lead to the possibility of using captures per session as a
> >cluster type variable. Maybe this is because he was doing direct
> >calculations and the program DISTANCE can account for this.
> >
> >I am going to rerun my data as individual records and see what happens.
> >
> >Barry
